parts.title: A new AI model that reads a virus's protein building blocks to sort viruses into their family groups
parts.abstract:
Abstract

Why we did this

Scientists sort viruses into a family tree with levels, from the broadest groups down to the narrowest. The International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV) keeps a carefully checked official version of this tree. Even so, only a small share of the viruses found by reading genetic material in large projects (such as studies of the viruses in the human body, or of the microbes living in soil and water) have a place in that tree. So we need methods that can place a virus at several levels at once. That way, a virus that is new at one level can still be placed in a broader group above it.

Some methods work by comparing a virus's genetic code with the codes of known viruses. They work well for viruses that are very similar to known ones, for example those in the same species or genus (a genus is a group of closely related species). But they do much worse for viruses that are more different. Recent deep-learning models, such as ViTax, try to solve this problem. ViTax uses a "DNA language model", a kind of AI that has learned the patterns of DNA. However, ViTax also does worse on new viruses that have no genus-level match among the known viruses it learned from.

Proteins change less over time than genetic codes do. A virus carries the instructions for many proteins, and these proteins can be used to reveal how viruses are related through evolution.

What we found

We built a new tool called D2T (Domain-to-Taxonomy) to help place viruses in the family tree. It uses recent progress in "protein language models", which are AI models that learn the patterns of proteins. D2T describes each virus as a list of its protein domains, which are the working parts of a protein, and treats each domain as a single word. It then learns a transformer, a type of AI model that reads a list of words and weighs how they relate to each other, to sort the virus into groups.

We tested D2T on several datasets. Some were "closed-set", meaning every virus in the test set belonged to a genus the model had already seen during training. Others were "open-set", meaning the test set included viruses from genera the model had never seen. D2T was excellent at giving labels at the higher levels of the tree, from family upward. We also combined D2T with Kraken2, a tool that is good at the genus level. This combined method, which we call K+D2T, sorts viruses accurately across several levels of the tree.

Where to find it

D2T is freely available on GitHub at https://github.com/mgtools/D2T.
parts.introduction_first:
Viruses are the most common and most varied living things on Earth. They infect every form of life and play key roles in evolution, in nature and in health. The virome (Wommack et al. 2012) is the complete collection of viruses in a given place, such as the human body, the oceans or the soil. It includes viruses that infect the cells of living things, and also phages, viruses that infect bacteria and help shape communities of microbes.

Today, scientists can read all the genetic material in a sample at once, a method called metagenomic sequencing, and analyse it with powerful computers. This has made virome projects possible (Delwart 2013). These projects aim to describe the variety of viruses in an orderly way, to uncover how viruses and the living things they infect affect each other, and to understand how viruses shape ecosystems and disease. The human virome is thought to be a central part of human health and disease (Gholamzad et al. 2024). It helps control how the immune system grows and responds, and it plays a crucial role in the development of diseases, including inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and Crohn's disease.
parts.introduction_rest:
Taxonomy, the science of naming and sorting living things, is essential for understanding how viruses are classified and how they evolve (Gorbalenya et al. 2020). Taxonomy arranges organisms into levels, from broad groups down to narrow ones, based on the features they share. It often follows a naming system that has been set in advance. For viruses, the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV) (Simmonds et al. 2023) creates the official family tree. It has eight levels, from the broadest to the narrowest: realm, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species. The ICTV builds this tree from how the viruses look, what kind of genetic material they carry, how they copy themselves, and how they are related through evolution. Because everyone uses the same system, viruses can be named and grouped in a consistent way.

Many viruses have been found by reading genetic material in large projects, and their codes have been stored in the NCBI database, a public online library of genetic information. Even so, sorting these viruses into the family tree has lagged behind. Other ways of classifying viruses exist, such as the Baltimore classification, which groups viruses by how they copy their genetic material and may not follow how they are related through evolution (Koonin et al. 2021).

One kind of method places a virus by comparing it with known viruses. Kraken2 (Wood et al. 2019) is one such tool. It works with short stretches of genetic code called k-mers, which are pieces of a fixed length, such as "ATCG". Instead of lining up whole genetic codes against each other, Kraken2 looks for exact matches of these short pieces. It first builds a kind of index from the genetic codes of known viruses. The index is made of "minimizers", which are the shortest stretches of code that contain at least one k-mer. For each minimizer, the index stores the Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) of the known viruses that contain it. The LCA is the closest shared ancestor of a set of viruses in the family tree.

To classify a new virus, Kraken2 pulls out its k-mers, looks up their minimizers in the index, and gathers the LCA answers into a score for each branch of the tree. Each k-mer "votes" for a branch, and the confidence score is the share of k-mer votes that support that branch. If the user sets a confidence threshold, Kraken2 gives the virus the narrowest level in the branch whose confidence score meets or passes that threshold. If no branch passes, the virus stays unclassified.

CAT (Von Meijenfeldt et al. 2019) uses a similar LCA approach, but it works with proteins instead of genetic code. It takes the stretches of a virus's genetic code that could be read as instructions for proteins, called open reading frames, and turns them into protein sequences. It then compares how similar these proteins are. How accurate these comparison-based methods are depends on how complete and accurate the reference collection of known viruses is, and on how well each virus in that collection has been classified.

Other methods use machine learning, where a computer learns patterns from examples. PhaGenus (Guan et al. 2023) is a transformer model that sorts phages (viruses that infect bacteria) into genera. It describes each phage by groups of similar proteins. ViTax (He et al. 2025) is a recently developed method built on HyenaDNA (Nguyen et al. 2023), a DNA language model that has learned general patterns of genetic code. ViTax was trained with a method called supervised prototypical contrastive learning. In this method, the model learns to give each virus a compact description, called an embedding, that is similar to the descriptions of viruses in the same group and different from those of other groups.

When ViTax classifies a new virus, it works step by step down the family tree, using a tree of LCA-based "beliefs" about which group each virus belongs to. It first tries to name the genus. If it is not confident enough, it steps back to a broader level, and keeps doing so until it finds a label it can trust. ViTax (He et al. 2025) was reported to do better than other existing methods, including Kraken2, CAT and PhaGenus. However, that comparison was made only on viruses whose genetic material is double-stranded DNA.

Placing viruses in the family tree is not easy, and there are several challenges. The tree has levels, and each level reflects how closely related viruses are through evolution. But viruses change quickly, and related viruses can quickly stop looking alike, especially at the level of their genetic code. Similarity between proteins can reveal more distant relationships, such as those at the genus level. Even so, working out relationships deeper in the tree, above the genus, is still hard, because no gene is shared by all viruses (Simmonds et al. 2023). For example, genes that help build the virus particle are useful for studying DNA viruses, while genes for the machinery that copies the genetic code are more useful for RNA viruses. On top of that, even the genes that are typical of a group, and the proteins they make, may change so much that they can no longer be reliably recognised and used to place viruses at the higher levels of the tree.

Recently developed protein language models have made many kinds of tasks possible, because they turn each protein into a description that captures how its parts relate to each other. Two widely used protein language models are ProtTrans (Elnaggar et al. 2022) and ESM-2 (Lin et al. 2023). ProtTrans was trained to produce descriptions that help with later tasks, such as predicting the local folds of a protein and where in the cell it works. ESM-2 was trained to produce descriptions that make it easier to predict a protein's 3D shape from its sequence alone.

We previously developed DCTdomain, which uses the descriptions made by ESM-2. Instead of describing a whole protein at once, DCTdomain first splits each protein into its domains, using maps from ESM-2 that predict which parts of the protein touch each other. It then turns the description of each building block in a domain into a list of numbers and applies a mathematical step called the discrete cosine transformation (DCT). This step combines the building blocks into a single description of the whole domain, which we call a domain fingerprint (Iovino et al. 2024). We previously showed that domain fingerprints can find distant relatives of proteins (Iovino et al. 2024).

In this paper, we develop D2T, a model that takes descriptions of protein domains as its input. It learns complex patterns that reflect how a virus's genetic code is organised into separate parts, and it uses these patterns to place viruses in the family tree. When we tested D2T against existing methods, it showed that information from protein domains can be used to place viruses accurately. This is especially true at the higher levels of the tree, above the genus, where the proteins of different viruses are not very similar.
parts.methods:
## 2 Methods

### 2.1 An overview of the model

Our method, D2T, describes a virus as a sentence made of protein domains, the working parts of its proteins (see Fig. 1 for a picture). D2T uses a transformer, a type of AI model that reads a list of words and weighs how they relate to each other. We added a second learning technique to it, called contrastive learning (see Fig. 2). We also propose a combined method that uses the strengths of D2T and of Kraken2, a tool that sorts viruses by comparing their genetic code with known viruses. Together they sort viruses accurately at every level of the family tree. We call this combined method K+D2T.

**Figure 1.** Using domain fingerprints to sort viruses into groups. Our transformer-based AI model, D2T, reads a virus as a list of domain tokens. In this drawing, each protein domain is a rectangle of a different colour. Gray arrows show genes. V1 and V2 are made-up (toy) virus genomes.

**Figure 2.** How D2T sorts viruses into groups. D2T is a transformer that reads a virus as a list of protein domain tokens and gives it a place in the family tree. It learns efficiently with two tricks: contrastive learning, and a scoring rule that takes the levels of the tree into account. (A) A virus's protein sequences are broken into domains, and the model reads these lists of domains. The model also makes a slightly changed copy of each list by randomly dropping some domains (domain dropout). A shared transformer reads both the original and the changed copy, and a step called gated attention pooling combines them into one final description of the virus. (B) The contrastive part pulls the description of a virus (the anchor) toward its changed copy (a strong positive) and toward viruses from the same genus (weak positives). It pushes away viruses from other groups (negatives). How far apart two viruses are in the tree (δij) decides how strongly they are pushed apart. (C) The model learns by combining two goals: sorting viruses at each level (Lclf) and contrastive learning (Lcon).

### 2.2 Describing a virus's genetic code as a list of domain tokens

For each virus's genetic code, we first find all the proteins it carries the instructions for. We then turn each protein into a domain fingerprint, a short list of numbers that describes its domains. D2T uses these fingerprints to place the virus in the family tree. To find the domains, we used a tool called DCTdomain (Iovino et al. 2024) on every protein in every virus's genetic code, and we turned each domain into a fingerprint.

This means that a domain of any length becomes a list of numbers of the same fixed size, for example 480 numbers. Using domains as the model's "words" has a practical advantage. A virus can then be described by a fairly short list of these words, instead of a very long list of single protein building blocks (amino acids). This way of describing proteins could matter when there are only a limited number of examples to learn from, which here means the number of viruses that have been given labels.

### 2.3 Reading the list of domains and combining it into one description

For each virus i, we build a list of domain tokens, Xi, and add extra "padding" tokens at the end so that every list has the same length. We also make a mask that marks which positions are padding and carry no real information. We then read Xi with a small transformer (Vaswani et al. 2017) that has 2 layers, 4 attention heads and a hidden size of dmodel = 480.

The transformer needs to know the order of the words in a list. Instead of giving each word a fixed position number, we used a method called rotary positional embeddings (Su et al. 2024). It works inside the transformer's attention step, which lets each word pay attention to the others. This lets the model handle lists of different lengths without storing exact positions. Each layer has several parts. It has multi-head self-attention, which lets each word look at all the others. It has a feed-forward block of size 2×dmodel, which does further calculations. It also has residual connections, which let the input pass through unchanged so that information is not lost. Finally, it has layer normalization, which keeps the numbers in a steady range, and dropout of 0.1, which randomly switches off 10% of the connections during training.

We then combine the outputs for all the tokens into a single description of the virus, zi, using gated attention pooling (Ilse et al. 2018). In this step, each token gets a weight that the model learns. The weight is made by passing the token's output through a tanh function and then through a sigmoid function, which squeezes the result into a range between 0 and 1. The weighted sum of all the tokens becomes zi. The padding tokens are left out during this step.

### 2.4 Learning from labelled examples with contrastive learning that respects the family tree

Sorting viruses into groups is hard for three reasons. The groups are arranged in levels, one inside another. Labels are limited, and some values are missing. And some groups have far more examples than others. To deal with these problems, we propose a scoring rule for contrastive learning that takes the levels of the tree into account. It is called a weighted margin NT-Xent loss.

To understand it, it helps to know what contrastive learning does. The model learns a description of each virus. It then checks whether the descriptions of related viruses are similar, and whether the descriptions of unrelated viruses are different. The NT-Xent loss is a common way to do this. It compares each description with all the others in the batch. The standard NT-Xent (Chen et al. 2020) treats all the "negative" pairs, meaning pairs that should be different, equally. Our version instead uses how far apart two viruses are in the tree to decide how much weight each negative pair gets. It also sets a different minimum gap, or margin, for pairs that are more or less distant in the tree.

For contrastive learning, we make two slightly changed copies of each virus's list of domains by randomly dropping some domains before the transformer reads it. Each copy is passed through the same transformer and pooling step, which share the same learned weights, to give two descriptions. These two descriptions form a strong positive pair. Each description then takes a turn as the "anchor", the description being checked. For each anchor, its partner copy is the strong positive. Viruses from the same genus are weak positives, and all the rest are negatives.

The sorting loss uses the description made from the original list, with no domains dropped. The contrastive loss uses the descriptions from the two copies. Before we measure how similar two descriptions are, we rescale each one so that its length is 1 (this is called ℓ2-normalizing).

#### 2.4.1 Measuring how far apart two viruses are in the tree, even when some labels are missing

We define a measure of distance in the family tree that still works when some labels are missing. Take any two viruses, i and j, each with labels at L levels of the tree. We look for the longest unbroken run of levels, starting from the broadest level (the realm), where both viruses have a label. Let Pij be the depth of this run of levels that are filled in for both viruses. Let Cij be the depth of their lowest common ancestor, the most specific group that both viruses belong to. The distance in the tree is then:

(1) δij = 1 − Cij/Pij, where δij is between 0 and 1.

A distance of 0 means the two viruses share the same group, and a distance of 1 means they share no group at all.

When there is not enough information (Pij = 0), we leave the pair out of the negatives. Even then, if both viruses have genus labels, we still count them as a positive pair if they belong to the same genus.

#### 2.4.2 How the contrastive loss takes the family tree into account

We change the contrastive learning setup by redefining which pairs count as positives and which as negatives, based on δij. Let zi be the rescaled description of virus i, and let Sij = zi · zj be the cosine similarity, a score of how similar two descriptions are. Here, each anchor i is one description (one copy) in the batch. Positives and negatives are defined with respect to this anchor. The changed loss for an anchor i is:

(2) Lcon,i = −log [ Σ over p in P(i) of ωip+ exp(sip/τ) ] / [ Σ over p in P(i) of ωip+ exp(sip/τ) + Σ over n in N(i) of ωin− exp((sin+min)/τ) ]

In practice, we calculate the top and bottom of this fraction with a method called logsumexp, which keeps the numbers from growing too large or too small for the computer to handle. We then average the loss over all anchors in the batch. Here, τ is the temperature, a setting that controls how sharply the model focuses on the strongest matches. The parts of the formula are defined as follows.

Positives (P): We make two slightly changed copies of each virus by dropping domains at random, and we treat each pair of copies as positives. Besides these changed copies, we also count as positives any viruses that share the same genus, when genus labels are available. Each kind of positive gets its own weight, ωip+: 1.0 for a changed copy and 0.5 for a genus match.

Negatives (N): The negatives are pairs of viruses that are different in the tree (δin > 0). Here, n stands for one member of the negative set N(i) for anchor i. We weight each negative pair by how far apart the two viruses are, using ωin− = exp(λ · δin). The number λ is a setting we choose, and it makes distant negatives count for more.

Distance-dependent margin (min): We add a margin, min, that changes the similarity rule depending on how far apart anchor i and negative n are in the tree. To set the margin, we sort the distances δin into K = L + 1 equal-width bins and map them onto a straight line from 0 to 1. We then add the margin to the similarity score of the negative pair. This acts as a penalty that makes the model keep more distant pairs further apart. So the bigger the biological distance, the stronger the separation in the model's descriptions. In this way, the similarity score of distant negatives is made to look higher than it really is, and the model has to push them further apart to make the loss as small as possible.

#### 2.4.3 The total goal

We train the model to do two things at once: learn good descriptions of viruses, and predict their place in the tree. The description zi of each virus is passed to a sorting part, gθ(ℓ), at each level ℓ of the tree. The sorting loss is a weighted average of cross-entropy losses across the levels, leaving out missing labels (marked as ⊥). Cross-entropy is a standard score of how wrong a model's guesses are.

We set the weights wℓ so that higher levels count for more, which keeps the model's predictions consistent with the structure of the tree (it predicts the higher levels more accurately). We also give the genus level a high weight, so that the model stays accurate at the narrowest level. We use fixed default weights wℓ = {0.18, 0.17, 0.15, 0.13, 0.11, 0.10, 0.16}, from realm down to genus, scaled so that they add up over the levels that have labels. We chose these weights by trial and error, to balance keeping the higher levels accurate against giving the model enough learning signal for the finer, harder levels. Fig. S1 compares how well different weight choices work.

Let Bℓ = {i | yi(ℓ) ≠ ⊥} be the set of viruses that have a label at level ℓ. A batch may contain no viruses with a label at a certain level. To handle this, we define the set of levels with at least one labelled virus as Lvalid = {ℓ | |Bℓ| > 0}. The sorting loss is then a weighted average over these levels:

(3) Lclf = (1 / Σ over ℓ in Lvalid of wℓ) · Σ over ℓ in Lvalid of wℓ · (1/|Bℓ|) · Σ over i in Bℓ of CE(gθ(ℓ)(zi), yi(ℓ)),

where CE is the cross-entropy loss.

The final goal combines the sorting loss and the contrastive loss:

(4) Ltotal = Lclf + αcon Lcon.

Here, αcon is a setting that controls how much the contrastive loss counts compared with the sorting loss.

### 2.5 The datasets we used for training and testing

We used the official labels from ICTV (Lefkowitz et al. 2018) as the correct answers for training and testing. We used several ICTV releases: MSL #38 (which we call MSL38 for short), MSL #39 release v4 (MSL39), and the most recent MSL #40 release v2 (MSL40). From these we built closed-set and open-set datasets. In the closed-set setting, the test viruses belong to genera that also appear in the training viruses. In the open-set setting, the test viruses come from new genera, meaning genera that do not appear in the training viruses.

To compare our methods fairly with ViTax (He et al. 2025) and other methods, we first used the closed-set and open-set datasets that had already been built from MSL38 (He et al. 2025). The training set has 2462 viruses, the closed-set test set has 1516, and the open-set test set has 785. This dataset contains only double-stranded DNA viruses.

We also built a new training and test dataset from MSL39, in a similar way to He et al. (2025), to test our new methods. Importantly, this dataset includes all the groups of viruses collected by ICTV. These include DNA viruses (Adnaviria, Duplodnaviria and Varidnaviria) and RNA viruses (Riboviria and Monodnaviria). We first put every genus represented by exactly one virus sample into the open-set part. We then shuffled the rest of the data at random and split it into training and test sets, aiming for a ratio of 3 to 2. In addition, for each level of the tree, we moved any test virus whose label at that level was missing from the training set into the training set, so that the test would be closed-set. The final dataset has 8590 training viruses, 5728 test viruses and 1899 open-set viruses. This new dataset is important for testing whether our methods work for all groups of viruses, not just double-stranded DNA viruses.

Finally, we built an open-set setting based on time, using the two most recent ICTV releases, to copy real-world use. Viruses that appear in MSL40 but were not in MSL39 are treated as open-set viruses, so the model never sees them during training. All 1563 virus samples in this MSL40 part belong to viral species that ICTV newly defined. To make the open-set test strict and clear-cut, we focused on viruses from genera that MSL40 newly defined. In total, MSL40 defines 238 new genera, and the 657 virus samples placed in these genera are the true open-set viruses in our tests. Fig. 3 shows how these new viruses are spread across the levels of the tree.

**Figure 3.** MSL39 training data compared with MSL40 open-set data containing new genera. The Venn diagrams compare which groups of viruses appear in the MSL39 training set and in the MSL40 open-set at each level of the tree. The numbers inside the diagrams are the number of different groups at that level. The numbers outside the diagrams, in the same colour, are the number of virus samples in each region. The numbers in brackets (ntrain, nopen) are the numbers of virus samples in the MSL39 training set and the MSL40 open-set that share groups in the overlap.

We used every virus sample that has a GenBank accession, a code that identifies a genetic sequence in the public GenBank database. For each accession, we downloaded the protein sequences from NCBI, the public database, using the accessions that ICTV provides. For accessions without protein sequences, we downloaded the genetic code instead and predicted the genes that code for proteins using a tool called prodigal-gv (v2.11.0) in metagenome mode (-p meta) (Hyatt et al. 2010, Camargo et al. 2024). We did this step because viruses have some unusual features, such as different genetic codes and gene structures that are common in giant viruses. We then used DCTdomain to make domain fingerprints for all the proteins, and these fingerprints are the input to our new method, D2T.

### 2.6 How we measured performance and compared with other methods

To measure how accurate each model is, we used standard scores for sorting tasks. Accuracy is the share of all viruses given the correct label. Balanced accuracy averages the accuracy over the different groups. Precision asks how many of the viruses a model placed in a group really belong there, and recall asks how many of the viruses that truly belong there the model found. Macro F1 combines precision and recall, giving each group equal weight. The Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) is a single score that takes into account all the right and wrong answers at once. Because virus labels are often incomplete, and not every virus sample has a label at every level, we left out the missing labels when calculating these scores.

To report fairly how the methods perform in the open-set setting, which reflects real-world use, we included the viruses from new groups and counted them as wrong, because they cannot be correctly predicted when the model only knows the groups it learned from. In the open-set setting, the test viruses come from new genera, meaning genera not seen in the training viruses. They may be new at one level but known at broader levels. For example, a new virus may be new all the way down to the order level (so it is new at the order, family and genus levels), while still being known at the realm, kingdom, phylum and class levels.

For the open-set cases, we also report an extra accuracy that includes only viruses known at a given level, even if they may be unknown at lower levels. This accuracy shows a more hopeful situation, when the model knows that a virus is new. Along with accuracy, we also report the share of the test viruses that are new, to show how hard the task is, because models tend to do worse when a larger share of the test viruses are new.

For comparison, we included two methods: ViTax (He et al. 2025), which learns from examples, and Kraken2 (Wood et al. 2019), which sorts viruses by comparing their genetic code with known viruses. We could not use the training code that comes with ViTax. So, to make a direct and fair comparison, we used the MSL38 dataset that had already been split, together with the ready-trained ViTax model released in the ViTax GitHub repository. This means our comparison with ViTax covers only the test sets built from MSL38. For Kraken2, we used the viruses in the training set to build reference databases, which Kraken2 compares the test viruses against. We compared our methods with Kraken2 on all the test sets.

### 2.7 The combined method, K+D2T

We noticed that our model, D2T, which reads a virus as a list of protein domains, is excellent at giving labels at the higher levels of the tree for viruses whose genetic code is not very similar to known viruses. But it may get confused at the genus level, where Kraken2 does well (see Results). To make the most of both methods, we built a simple combined method, K+D2T. It runs Kraken2 first and applies D2T only to the viruses that Kraken2 could not sort.

We also tried other tools that sort viruses by comparing their genetic code with known viruses. In particular, we tested skani (Shaw and Yu 2023), a recently developed tool that quickly calculates average nucleotide identity (ANI), a measure of how similar two genetic codes are. We wanted to see whether skani could be used to place viruses that are quite similar to known genera. We found that simply passing on labels based on the calculated ANI worked worse than Kraken2. So in this study, we use Kraken2 both for comparison and for combining with D2T.

### 2.8 Understanding what the models learned

To understand D2T's predictions, we used two kinds of scores that show which parts of the input the model relied on (Lundberg and Lee 2017). One kind comes from the transformer's attention, which shows how much each word pays attention to each other word. The other kind is SHapley Additive exPlanations, or SHAP (Lundberg and Lee 2017), which shows how much each part of the input pushes the model's answer up or down.

We used these scores to estimate how much each protein contributes to the model's prediction. To get a score for a protein, we add up the SHAP values of all its domains. This shows how much that protein moves the model's prediction toward or away from a particular label. Proteins with large positive SHAP values give strong support for the predicted label, while proteins with values close to zero have little influence on the decision. As a result, the proteins that rank highest can be seen as possible marker proteins, which capture patterns in the sequence or domains that are special to a particular line of viruses and that the model has learned. We calculated these scores using gradient SHAP from the Captum API (Kokhlikyan et al. 2009).

### 2.9 How we built the tools and where to find them

We built D2T in the Python programming language using PyTorch (Paszke et al. 2019). We used scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al. 2011) to split the data into K parts, called folds, for K-fold cross-validation. In this method, the model is trained on all but one fold and tested on the fold left out, and this is repeated so that each fold gets a turn. We add padding to the lists of domain tokens so that they can be processed in batches, and the padding mask keeps the padding out of the attention and pooling steps. We fixed the random seed to 42, so that anyone running our code gets exactly the same results. With the data already split, we did 5-fold cross-validation only on the training set. We then chose the saved version of the model with the lowest score on the validation data, and used it for the final test on the held-out test set.

We ran our experiments on NVIDIA A40 graphics cards (46 GB of memory each). On this hardware, training the model on all the viruses in the MSL39 dataset takes up to 9 hours, depending on how many epochs (full passes through the training data) the model needs before we stop training early. To sort a new virus, the steps first use DCTdomain to make domain fingerprints from the protein sequences. This step takes some computing power, but it is still reasonably fast. For example, it took 65 minutes for the 79 222 proteins carried by the 657 new viruses from MSL40, or about 0.05 seconds per protein. With these fingerprints, D2T then sorts the virus quickly, taking about 6 seconds for the same 657 viruses.

We tuned the model's settings by hand on the MSL38 dataset, using only the training and validation folds. We then used the same settings for the MSL39 dataset without tuning them again. We trained for up to 200 epochs with batches of 32 viruses, using a training method called AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter 2017), with a learning rate of 10−4 and a weight decay of 10−4. The learning rate controls how big a step the model takes each time it adjusts itself. We lowered it whenever the score on the validation data stopped improving for 5 epochs in a row (a setting called ReduceLROnPlateau, with a factor of 0.1 and a minimum learning rate of 10−6). We stopped training early if the score did not improve for 10 epochs in a row. The total goal uses αcon = 0.05. For contrastive learning, we used a temperature τ = 0.1, domain dropout of 0.1 to make the two slightly changed copies, logsumexp aggregation, and negative weighting exp(λδij) with λ = 1.0. Fig. S2 shows how the results change when we change these settings. We set the distance-dependent margins by rounding δij into L + 1 bins and mapping them onto a straight line from 0 to 1.

The D2T models we trained, along with the programs for training and testing, are available in a GitHub repository at https://github.com/mgtools/D2T. All the training and test datasets are also available in the D2T repository.

## 3 Results

### 3.1 How well the models did on double-stranded DNA viruses

We start with the results for datasets that contain only double-stranded DNA viruses. These are viruses whose genetic material is DNA, with two strands twisted together.

Table 1 compares our two methods, D2T and K+D2T, with two existing tools, ViTax and Kraken2. All four were tested on the closed-set of double-stranded DNA viruses built from MSL38, a large collection of virus samples. We think this test set is fairly easy. Every virus in it belongs to a genus that also appears in the training set, the examples the models learned from. As the results show, all the models made accurate predictions at every level of the family tree.

### 3.2 How well the models did on all six realms of viruses

Next, we tested the models on all viruses from the different realms, including both DNA and RNA viruses. A realm is the broadest level of the virus family tree. We wanted to see whether our methods still work well on such a varied mix of viruses, covering all six realms of DNA and RNA viruses. For this test, we built the training and test datasets from MSL39 and MSL40.

Table 3 shows the results on the MSL39 closed-set, where the viruses in the test set share genera with those used for training. Compared with the results for double-stranded DNA viruses alone (Table 1), Kraken2 did much worse. For example, its accuracy at the realm level fell from 0.973 to 0.774. This shows that placing viruses in the tree is harder when they are not double-stranded DNA viruses. D2T, in contrast, stayed strong. It reached near-perfect accuracy at every level (above 0.95), except at the genus level, where its accuracy was 0.791. By combining the strengths of D2T and Kraken2, K+D2T reached a genus-level accuracy of 0.865 (Table 3).

### 3.3 Using attention scores to find the proteins that help place a virus in the tree

One possible advantage of using D2T to place viruses in the tree is that we can use its attention scores. These scores show how much each protein domain contributes to the model's decision, so we can learn how much each protein matters for placing a virus in the tree. Figure 6 shows how D2T placed a few DNA viruses, to show that the model's decisions can be understood.

Figure 6

Examples showing that D2T's decisions can be understood. Three typical examples show how D2T picks out how much each protein contributes to placing a virus in the tree. In each panel, the virus's genes are shown as boxes along the bottom, in alternating black and grey. Wider boxes are longer genes, and the labels along the bottom show where each gene sits in the genome. The bar chart above shows how important each protein is. Arrows point to the two proteins that contribute most to placing each virus in the tree, and their jobs are given. Green triangles mark DNA polymerases.

The first example is Staphylococcus phage Andhra (isolate ID = 1002333) (Cater et al. 2017). Its genome is 18 546 base pairs long (base pairs are the "letters" of DNA), and it carries the instructions for 28 proteins. It belongs to the realm Duplodnaviria, the kingdom Heunggongvirae and the genus Andhravirus. The two proteins that contributed most to placing this virus in the tree are a peptidase (protein ID: AQT27832), an enzyme that cuts proteins, and the major capsid protein (AQT27840), the main building block of the virus's outer shell.

The second example is Staphylococcus phage St 134 (Golosova et al. 2024). Here, the protein that helps wrap the virus's genetic material into its shell (the encapsidation protein) contributed most to placing it in the tree, followed by the major capsid protein.

The third example is Enterococcus phage AE4_17. It infects E. faecalis bacteria that resist antibiotics, which were collected from infected root canals (El-Telbany et al. 2021). The protein that contributed most is the terminase large subunit. In many viruses, this is a key enzyme that helps pack the virus's DNA: it fills empty virus shells with the virus's DNA.

In all three examples, capsid proteins and terminases were among the most important proteins D2T found for placing the virus in the tree. This matches earlier research, which shows that the parts of a virus that build its outer shell are good features for telling DNA viruses apart (Simmonds et al. 2023). DNA polymerases, the enzymes that copy DNA, were among the largest proteins these viruses carry, yet they contributed less to placing the viruses in the tree. This also matches earlier findings. Genes for copying the genome are generally not good for defining the realms of large DNA viruses, because even closely related viruses in the same realm often have different ways of copying their DNA.

### 3.4 Testing which parts of the model matter

We ran an ablation study to see how two choices affect D2T's performance. An ablation study means building the model in different versions, each missing or changed in one part, and comparing how well each version does. The first choice was the encoder, the part of the model that turns the list of protein domains into a description of the virus. The second was the contrastive loss, a training method that teaches the model to tell apart viruses that belong to different groups.

To make the comparison fair, every version used exactly the same settings, such as the learning rate (how big a step the model takes each time it adjusts itself) and the batch size (how many examples it looks at at once). We compared a simple encoder, called an MLP (multi-layer perceptron), with a transformer encoder, both set up in the same way and both trained with contrastive loss. We also compared a transformer encoder trained with contrastive loss against the same encoder trained without it. Table 5 shows the results on the MSL38 closed-set.

The transformer encoder did better than the MLP encoder at every level, and adding contrastive loss helped. The transformer encoder trained with contrastive loss scored better on every measure than the same encoder trained without it. These results show that combining a transformer encoder with contrastive loss gives the most reliable descriptions of viruses for placing them in the tree.

We also tested whether skani, a recently developed tool that quickly calculates average nucleotide identity (ANI), could be used to place viruses in the tree at the genus level. ANI measures how alike the genetic codes of two viruses are, on average. We used skani's search results (with the -n 1 option) to find the single reference virus that best matches each query virus, based on ANI. We then gave the query virus the same label as that best match.

It is important to note that skani has strict built-in filters. It throws out matches where less than 15% of the genetic code lines up, or where the ANI is below 80%. Query viruses that did not meet these limits got no result, and we counted them as wrong answers. When we tested skani on the MSL38 closed-set, it did not give good results. At the genus level, skani reached an accuracy of 0.774, a large drop compared with the 0.935 that Kraken2 reached on the MSL38 closed-set. For this reason, we compared our methods only with Kraken2 above, and we built our combined approach using Kraken2.
parts.discussion:
## 4 Discussion: what our results mean

We used domain fingerprints, which are short lists of the protein domains a virus carries, to build our D2T model. With them, D2T placed viruses accurately at several levels of the family tree, and across different groups of viruses, both those that carry their genetic material as DNA and those that carry it as RNA. D2T does especially well at the higher levels of the tree. This is where methods that rely on genetic code tend to do worse. Some of these methods compare how similar a virus's genetic code is to known viruses, such as Kraken2. Others use DNA language models, such as ViTax.

Even though D2T predicts labels very accurately, there is still room to improve. In some test cases, and especially in open-set tests, two measures of performance stayed fairly low. The first is balanced accuracy, which is the average of how often the model gets each group right. The second is the F1 score, which combines how many of the viruses in a group the model finds with how many of the viruses it names as that group really belong there. These scores are likely low because of class imbalance, meaning that some groups have far more examples than others. Training the model with more examples from rare groups, and fewer from the most common ones, may help it perform better. We also plan to add confidence scores, which would show how sure the model is about each label. These would let us flag inputs that are unlike anything the model has seen, and help it tell apart new groups of viruses.

In this work, we used a simple way to combine the strengths of Kraken2 and D2T, so that the two tools make up for each other's weak points and together sort viruses accurately at every level. Lower levels, such as the genus, benefit from methods that compare genetic code, like Kraken2. Higher levels benefit from D2T, which captures how the protein domains fit together and what they do.

When we looked at the viruses that were labelled wrongly, we found that having only a few examples of a group may have caused some of the confident mistakes at every level (see Tables S1 and S2). At the same time, mistakes at the genus level often happened even when a group had many examples. This suggests that domain fingerprints may be good at capturing broad signals of how viruses are related through evolution, but may miss the fine details in the order of protein building blocks that are needed to tell genera apart. This difference is one more reason why we needed our combined K+D2T approach.

It may be worth trying other methods that compare genetic code, including a tool called skani, to build more accurate combined methods. Skani was mainly designed to quickly calculate average nucleotide identity (ANI), which measures how closely the genetic code of two viruses matches. So our current approach, which simply picks the closest match in the training data, may not make full use of what skani can do. Another promising direction is to build a single model for sorting viruses at every level. It would bring together two kinds of information: domain-level features that help with the higher levels, and fine-grained features of the genetic code (or of the protein building blocks) that are essential for sorting viruses into genera.
